extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, respondents/appellants in USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) proceedings, and counsel handling USPTO disciplinary appeals
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing requests for reconsideration of USPTO Director final orders in OED disciplinary matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)), including what counts as 'new evidence', limits on relitigation, evidentiary waiver rules, jurisdictional principles, and examples of conduct found sanctionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for Reconsideration under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for reconsideration or modification of a Director's final decision may be filed within twenty days of the decision and will be granted only if based on newly discovered evidence, or an error of law or fact; the requester must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation's plain terms govern; the requester bears the burden to show new evidence or an error of law/fact. Requests are not vehicles to reargue an unsuccessful appeal. See quoted regulatory language and discussion in the Final Order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow standard of review (analogous to Fed. R. Civ. P. 59(e)/60)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard applied to § 11.56(c) requests is narrow and limited to circumstances involving new evidence or correcting errors of law or fact, analogous to motions under Federal Rules 59(e) and 60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal case law (e.g., Hutchinson v. Staton; Boryan v. United States) is useful guidance: mere disagreement or relitigation does not justify reconsideration. Courts treat such motions as extraordinary relief reserved for extraordinary circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newly discovered evidence must be previously unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence proffered as 'new' must not have been available prior to entry of the final decision and could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the Order: a Petition to Revive filed and granted before the disciplinary hearing is not 'new'; state malpractice court documents served on the appellant prior to the hearing are not 'new'. Case citations: Boryan, Wyle v. Texaco. The requester must affirmatively show why evidence was not and could not have been discovered earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is not for relitigation or mere disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: A request for reconsideration cannot be used to relitigate issues already decided, rehash previously presented arguments, or present evidence/arguments that could have been raised earlier; mere disagreement does not support reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Hutchinson, Arthur v. King, Wadley v. Park at Landmark, Above the Belt v. Mel Bohannan Roofing. Reconsideration appropriate only where the court/agency misunderstood a party, acted outside the issues, or made an apprehension error—not to give an unhappy party another chance to sway the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary remedy — motions granted sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for reconsideration under § 11.56(c) are extraordinary remedies and should be granted only in extraordinary circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited support: Dowell v. State Farm; Projects Mgmt. Co. v. DynCorp; Netscape v. ValueClick. The Order emphasizes the high bar and that such relief is rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED disciplinary jurisdiction over registered practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent practitioner registered with the USPTO is subject to the Office's disciplinary authority; claims that OED lacked subject-matter jurisdiction are inappropriate where the respondent is a registered practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order treats registration (e.g., since March 3, 1971) as incontrovertible basis for jurisdiction and rejects attempts to relitigate jurisdiction when provided for by regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of evidentiary objections if not raised timely
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party fails to object to the admission of evidence at the time it is introduced, objections are waived and cannot later be used as a basis for reversal or reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: appellant's limited, untimely objections to testimony were deemed waived because most testimony and the document were admitted without contemporaneous objection. Case cited: MicroStrategy Inc. v. Business Objects, S.A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial evidence supports ALJ findings — deference to factfinding
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director will not overturn an ALJ's factual findings if there is substantial evidence in the record to support them (e.g., witnesses' testimony and documentary evidence supporting conclusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order notes that even excluding the small portion of testimony for which objection was sustained, sufficient admissible evidence remained to support the ALJ's finding (e.g., settlement agreement, Ms. Chaiken's testimony). This reflects agency deference to ALJ factfinding where record support exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with appellate/filing requirements is mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are expected to comply with USPTO filing requirements (page limits, formatting, etc.); failure to do so after multiple opportunities can be an independent basis for rejecting an appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellant's claimed unfair constraint by filing requirements is not a basis for reconsideration when the rules apply equally and the party failed to file a compliant brief despite opportunities. See November 2016 Order denying waiver request and cited authority Fetrow-Fix v. Harrah Entm't.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of professional misconduct warranting discipline (specific regulatory violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct found to violate USPTO professional rules includes: failing to timely inform client of important prosecution events (e.g., third rejection, Board decision, notice of abandonment), neglecting a patent application for extended period, refusing to communicate with a client about matter status, and refusing to return a client's file when requested (violations cited under 37 C.F.R. §§ 10.23(a),(b), 10.23(c)(8), 10.77(c), 10.84(a)(1)&(2), 10.112(c)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory/regulatory citations were the basis for the ALJ's misconduct findings and the discipline ordered (eight-month suspension conditioned on MPRE). The Order treats such conduct as sanctionable and appropriately considered in assessing discipline and aggravating factors (e.g., attempted obstruction via settlement clause).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempted obstruction / agreements limiting witness cooperation as aggravating conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to include settlement provisions that would prevent client personnel from testifying or participating in disciplinary investigations (unless modified) can constitute 'bad faith obstruction' and are an aggravating factor in imposing discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order summarizes that advocating for a settlement clause to prohibit testimony was found to be intended to hinder disciplinary investigations; evidence included draft settlement and related witness testimony. The ALJ treated this as aggravating when determining sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural timelines for seeking judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Appellant is entitled to seek judicial review on the record in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 35 U.S.C. § 32 within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural right notice included at the conclusion of the Order; parties should follow local rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) when seeking judicial review.
